scope: All 9 canonical records currently carrying reviewStatus=outdated

policy.recalledAnswer: Preserved exactly; never overwritten by current guidance.
policy.verifiedAnswer: Not assigned in this review file unless the current evidence clearly supports a source option as the modern answer.
policy.sourceVsCurrent: Historical exam logic is kept separate from contemporary clinical practice.
policy.nextStep: Canonical records should be updated only after the evidence note below is merged into each record; questions with no modern correct listed option remain non-publishable.

items.currentPreferredConcept: Hydroxocobalamin is the preferred empiric cyanide antidote for severe smoke-inhalation cyanide poisoning where indicated; sodium thiosulfate is not the preferred stand-alone modern answer.
items.reason: The only retained option is historical and does not represent the preferred contemporary antidote.

items.recalledAnswer: B — moderate intellectual disability from mental-age/IQ calculation
items.currentPreferredConcept: Diagnosis and severity assessment require intellectual functioning plus adaptive functioning; severity is based primarily on adaptive-function deficits rather than a mental-age ratio or IQ alone.
items.reason: The stem does not provide enough adaptive-function information to assign a current severity category.

items.currentPreferredConcept: Current diagnostic pathways prioritize anti-AChR/other appropriate antibody testing and electrodiagnostic testing such as repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG in the appropriate clinical context; edrophonium is not the preferred modern next test.
items.reason: The source preserves only edrophonium, while current Saudi/GCC consensus uses serologic and electrodiagnostic pathways.

items.currentPreferredConcept: Use the current Saudi MOH catch-up/routine schedule and prior valid doses; do not use a fixed historical product list as timeless guidance.
items.reason: The option names/products include historical pneumococcal wording and the exact Saudi catch-up combination cannot be safely inferred from an old recall.

items.currentPreferredConcept: Both HIV and sickle cell disease are pneumococcal risk conditions. Current recommendations use PCV15/PCV20 and may use PPSV23 depending age and prior PCV history; PPSV23 itself is not a context-free single-answer rule.
items.reason: The 18-month sickle-cell option is below the PPSV23 minimum age, but the 13-year-old HIV option still requires prior vaccine history to determine whether PPSV23 is indicated; the stem is insufficient for current guidance.

items.currentPreferredConcept: For a dirty/puncture wound, a booster is indicated when at least 5 years have passed since the last tetanus-containing dose in a person with a completed primary series. At age 11 years, Tdap is preferred if the person has not previously received Tdap or Tdap history is unknown.
items.reason: The need for a booster is supported, but the modern preferred product (Tdap) is absent from the source options.

items.currentPreferredConcept: DKA-related cerebral injury is multifactorial. ISPAD notes that rapid fluid/osmolality change was the earlier theory, whereas more recent evidence points to cerebral hypoperfusion and DKA-related hyperinflammation as central mechanisms; cerebral edema correlates with dehydration/hyperventilation rather than osmotic change during treatment.
items.reason: None of the listed options adequately represents the current mechanistic understanding, so the historical answer A should not be auto-graded as current medicine.

items.currentPreferredConcept: The phenotype plus urinary phenylpyruvate historically points to PKU/PAH deficiency, but ferric chloride urine testing is a legacy diagnostic method. Current care relies on newborn screening, quantitative phenylalanine assessment and confirmatory/genotype-guided evaluation.
items.reason: The diagnosis represented by option A remains compatible with the described historical finding, but the question teaches an obsolete diagnostic test and should be labeled legacy rather than presented as a modern work-up.

items.currentPreferredConcept: Sudden cardiac death during stimulant therapy is extremely rare, and stimulants have not been shown to increase sudden-death risk above that of unexposed children. Common adverse effects include appetite loss, abdominal pain, headache and sleep disturbance; cardiac history/risk assessment remains important.
items.reason: The source keeps only one option and frames an extremely rare event as the defining 'most concerning' adverse effect, which is not a sound current single-best-answer item.

summary.recommendedNextAction: Apply these evidence notes to canonical records, keeping eight items non-publishable and retaining Metabolic Q5 as a verified diagnosis with an explicit legacy-test warning.
